author: Epiphanius of Salamis
occasion: Epiphanius writes to the emperor to oppose the painting of images of Christ and the saints in churches and on door curtains, and to urge their removal.
argument: Epiphanius argues that the devil introduced idolatry into the world and is now deceiving believers back into it through painted images. He claims no ancient father or bishop painted Christ or the saints, and that those who do so dishonor Christ and invent false appearances from their own imagination. He argues that painters wrongly depict Christ with long hair by confusing 'Nazorean' with 'Nazirite', even though Christ drank wine, which Nazirites did not. He further argues that if Christ had distinctive long hair while the other disciples were shorn, the Pharisees and scribes would not have needed Judas to identify him with a kiss. He concludes by asking that curtains with such images be used for burying the poor, wall paintings be whitewashed, and images already painted in a shrine be removed if possible, with no new images painted.

outline.move: Epiphanius introduces himself, states that the devil has led believers back into idolatry through images, affirms his adherence to the faith of the Nicene fathers, and asks whether it is fitting to have a painted God.

He asks which ancient fathers or bishops dishonored Christ by painting him or the saints, argues that painters falsely invent appearances, and refutes the depiction of Christ with long hair by distinguishing 'Nazorean' from 'Nazirite' and noting that Christ drank wine.

He shows that painters contradict each other in depicting Peter and Paul and depict the other disciples as shorn, then argues that if Christ had distinctive long hair while the disciples were shorn, the Pharisees and scribes would not have needed Judas's kiss to identify him.

He reports that he was treated as a laughingstock and that his fellow bishops and fellow ministers refused to remove the images, and he requests that curtains with such images be used for burying the poor, wall paintings be whitewashed, and images in a shrine be removed if possible, with no new images painted.

key_terms.sense: Idolatry, the worship of images as gods
A painted image or portrait, especially of Christ or the saints
Curtains or veils, especially door curtains in churches bearing images
Nazirites, those under a vow involving uncut hair and abstinence from wine
Nazorean, a title for Jesus that painters mistakenly connect with Nazirite hair customs
Long hair, used in the argument about Christ's appearance
Forms or appearances of the saints invented by painters
Fellow ministers or fellow bishops with whom Epiphanius serves
A small shrine or chapel where images had already been painted

scripture: The letter does not cite specific biblical books by name, but refers to figures from the Old and New Testaments (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, the prophets, Peter, Andrew, James, John, the apostles, Judas, the Pharisees and scribes). Psalm numbering is not used.
uncertain: The exact date of the letter
The identity of the specific Theodosius addressed (Theodosius I or Theodosius II)
The precise meaning of μουσαρίῳ (possibly a shrine, chapel, or tomb structure)

_unresolved_facts.claim: Epiphanius writes to the emperor to oppose the painting of images of Christ and the saints in churches and on door curtains, and to urge their removal.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἤκουσα ὡς καὶ τὸν ἀκατάληπτον υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ τινὲς γράφειν ἐπαγγέλλονται
_unresolved_facts.fix: Epiphanius writes to the emperor to oppose the painting of images of God the Father (τὸν ἀκατάληπτον υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ — 'the incomprehensible Son of God' is disputed; the text says he heard some promise to paint even the incomprehensible Son of God), and of Christ and the saints, and to urge their removal.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He claims no ancient father or bishop painted Christ or the saints
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τίς τῶν παλαιῶν πατέρων Χριστοῦ εἰκόνα ζωγραφήσας ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ ἢ ἐν οἴκῳ ἰδίῳ κατέθετο ἢ ἐν βήλοις θυρῶν; τίς τῶν ἀρχαίων ἐπισκόπων Χριστὸν ἀτιμάσας ἐζωγράφησεν;
_unresolved_facts.fix: He asks rhetorically which ancient fathers or bishops painted Christ's image in a church or private house or on door curtains, or dishonored Christ by painting him — implying none did, but using interrogative form rather than direct claim.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He argues that painters wrongly depict Christ with long hair by confusing 'Nazorean' with 'Nazirite', even though Christ drank wine, which Nazirites did not.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: κόμην γὰρ ἔχοντα τὸν σωτῆρα γράφουσιν ἐξ ὑπονοίας διὰ τὸ Ναζωραῖον αὐτὸν καλεῖσθαι, ἐπείπερ οἱ Ναζιραῖοι κόμας ἔχουσιν. Σφάλλονται δὲ οἱ τοὺς τύπους αὐτῷ συνάπτειν πειρώμενοι· οἶνον γὰρ ἔπινεν ὁ σωτήρ, ὃν οἱ Ναζιραῖοι οὐκ ἔπινον.
_unresolved_facts.fix: He reports that painters depict the Savior with long hair, conjecturing from his being called 'Nazorean' because Nazirites have long hair; then he notes they err who try to connect these types, since the Savior drank wine, which Nazirites did not. The drinking wine point is a separate refutation of the Nazirite connection, not directly about the hair depiction.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Epiphanius introduces himself, states that the devil has led believers back into idolatry through images, affirms his adherence to the faith of the Nicene fathers, and asks whether it is fitting to have a painted God.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: εἰσφέρει ἑαυτὸν ἐν τῇ ἐπιστολῇ τῇ πίστει τῶν ἐν Νικαίᾳ πατέρων ἐκ νέας ἡλικίας ἠκολουθηκέναι καὶ ὡς οἱ γονεῖς αὐτοῦ ἐν ταύτῃ γεγέννηνται καὶ τὴν αὐτὴν εἶχον ὁμολογίαν
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text reports (third-person) that Epiphanius presents himself in the letter as having followed the faith of the Nicene fathers from youth, and that his parents were born in it and held the same confession — this is narrative summary, not Epiphanius's first-person introduction.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He reports that he was treated as a laughingstock
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὁμολογεῖ, πρῶτα μὲν ὡς χλεύη τοῖς πολλοῖς ἐπὶ τοῖς ληρῳδουμένοις αὐτῷ προὔκειτο
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text reports (third-person) that he confesses/admits first that mockery from the many was directed at him for the nonsense talked against him — 'ληρῳδουμένοις αὐτῷ' means 'the nonsense spoken against him,' not that he was treated as a laughingstock for his own position.

_unresolved_facts.claim: his fellow bishops and fellow ministers refused to remove the images
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὅτι πολλάκις λαλήσας τοῖς συλλειτουργοῖς μου περιαιρεθῆναι τὰς εἰκόνας οὐκ ἐδέχθην παρ' αὐτῶν οὐδὲ πρὸς βραχὺ ἀκοῦσαι τῆς ἐμῆς φωνῆς ἠνέσχοντο
_unresolved_facts.fix: he was not received by them, nor did they endure to hear his voice even briefly — the text says they would not listen to him, not specifically that they 'refused to remove the images' (the refusal to listen is emphasized, not a direct refusal to act).

_unresolved_facts.claim: Theodosius, source_forms: ["Θεοδόσιον τὸν βασιλέα"], who: "The emperor to whom the letter is addressed"
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἐπιφανίου ἐπισκόπου Κύπρων Ἐπιστολὴ πρὸς Θεοδόσιον τὸν βασιλέα
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source gives the title as 'Epistula ad Theodosium imperatorem' / 'Ἐπιστολὴ πρὸς Θεοδόσιον τὸν βασιλέα' but the body of the letter does not address Theodosius directly; the addressee is in the title only, and the letter body appears to be third-person narrative about Epiphanius's letter rather than the letter itself.

_unresolved_facts.claim: First-person authorial voice throughout the letter
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: εἰσφέρει ἑαυτὸν ἐν τῇ ἐπιστολῇ... ὁμολογεῖ... εὕρομεν ἐν τῷ τέλει τῆς ἐπιστολῆς
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source text is largely third-person narrative about Epiphanius's letter (εἰσφέρει, ὁμολογεῖ, εὕρομεν), not first-person authorial voice. The first-person voice appears only in quoted material from the letter itself (e.g., 'τοῖς συλλειτουργοῖς μου').
